title: NASA Chooses Team to Investigate Lunar Cave Systems for Future Moon Exploration
body:
NASA has awarded a $2.4 million contract to a research team led by the Planetary Science Institute (PSI) to study a mysterious pit on the Moon that may open onto a vast underground cavern. The project, part of the agency’s Lunar Exploration Program, will use high‑resolution imaging, radar data and computer modeling to determine whether the pit—known as “Mare Tranquillitatis Pit”—connects to a larger subsurface void that could one day serve as a natural shelter for astronauts on future lunar bases.

The investigation comes at a time when NASA’s Artemis missions are gearing up to return humans to the Moon and establish a sustainable presence. While surface habitats will be protected by regolith shielding and advanced materials, radiation exposure and micrometeoroid impacts remain persistent hazards. A natural cave, if it exists, could provide a ready‑made refuge, reducing the mass and cost of building thick protective walls. “Lunar lava tubes and pits are the most promising real estate for human outposts because they offer inherent protection from the harsh environment,” said Dr. Megan R. Scully, principal investigator for the PSI team.

The selected study will combine data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter’s Narrow Angle Camera, the Diviner thermal imager, and the Lunar Radar Sounder to map the pit’s dimensions and subsurface structure. By analyzing shadows, temperature fluctuations and radar reflections, researchers hope to infer the depth and continuity of any hidden chambers. The team will also develop 3D models to simulate how a cavern might have formed through volcanic processes billions of years ago, when the Moon’s interior was still active enough to carve extensive lava tubes.

If the pit proves to be the entrance to a larger cavity, the findings could reshape NASA’s approach to lunar architecture. Current habitat designs rely on deploying inflatable modules or constructing habitats from locally sourced regolith. A natural cavern would dramatically cut down on the amount of material needed to be launched from Earth, allowing more payload capacity for scientific equipment and life‑support systems. Moreover, the stable temperatures inside a lava tube—typically ranging from –20 °C to +20 °C—would lessen the energy required for heating and cooling, making long‑duration stays more feasible.

The study also holds implications beyond the Moon. Similar volcanic features have been identified on Mars, and the techniques refined by the PSI team could be applied to future Martian missions seeking shelter from radiation and dust storms. Additionally, the research aligns with international interest in using extraterrestrial caves for scientific exploration, as they may preserve ancient geological records and even trap volatile compounds that could inform our understanding of the solar system’s evolution.

The PSI team will deliver a comprehensive report to NASA by early 2028, outlining the pit’s geometry, the likelihood of an adjoining cavern, and recommendations for potential robotic or crewed exploration. Should the results be favorable, the agency could prioritize the site for a future Artemis lander mission, integrating it into a broader network of lunar habitats. As humanity prepares to step back onto the Moon, the prospect of natural underground sanctuaries could prove pivotal in turning a temporary foothold into a lasting presence.
